list.listitem: Pneumonia is suggested in children with fever, tachypnea, hypoxia, retractions, and nasal flaring, but no single sign or symptom can determine if a child has pneumonia. C
Children with suspected bacterial pneumonia should be treated with antibiotics (see ). A

If considering C. trachomatis, young infants should be treated with a macrolide; children aged 3 months to 18 years with bacterial pneumonia should be treated with high-dose amoxicillin to cover S. pneumoniae. B

Macrolide antibiotics should be prescribed for children with findings compatible with pneumonia caused by atypical pathogens, if there is no response to first-line empirical antibiotics, and considered as an additional antibiotic in those with severe disease. B

background.definition: Community-acquired pneumonia is an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma in a patient who has acquired the infection in the community.

list.listitem: In the developed world, age younger than 5 years: 30/1000 to 45/1000 persons/year.
Decreases with age so that by adolescence: 6/1000 to 12/1000 persons/year.
Single biggest cause of death in children worldwide.
Age younger than 1 month: not within the scope of this topic.

Age 1 month to 3 months: may have afebrile pneumonia of infancy caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, respiratory syncytial virus, other respiratory viruses, Bordetella pertussis, cytomegalovirus, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes.

Age 4 months to 5 years: respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, and other respiratory viruses; Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes.
Age 6 years to 18 years: S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, respiratory viruses such as influenza and non-typeable H. influenzae.
Severe pneumonia in all ages is more likely due to S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, group A streptococci, H. influenzae, M. pneumoniae, or adenovirus.

In a study of 7509 otherwise healthy children hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia, one-third had a blood culture, of which only 2.5% grew a pathogen (primarily S. pneumoniae sensitive to penicillin).
In children at risk for aspiration, oral flora (anaerobic streptococci, fusobacterium, prevotella) should also be considered.
In hospitalized and immunocompromised children, gram-negative organisms and S. aureus should be considered more strongly.
Eight percent to 40% of community-acquired pneumonia cases are a mixed infection.
H. influenzae type b (Hib) is an unlikely cause of community-acquired pneumonia in children who have completed a primary series of Hib vaccinations.
Pneumococcal vaccines have decreased the incidence of pneumonia; however, S. pneumoniae remains the most common cause of bacterial pneumonia.
Pneumonia often follows an upper respiratory infection, which allows invasion of the lower respiratory tract by pathogens that trigger the immune response and produce inflammation.
Reduce smoke exposure. The incidence of pneumonia is two times higher in children of parents who smoke. A
Vaccinations against H. influenzae type b, B. pertussis, influenza, and S. pneumoniae are recommended.A
Hand washing and good personal hygiene are important preventative measures. C

A systematic review identified risk factors associated with severe acute lower respiratory infections in children younger than 5 years of age: low birth weight (OR: 3.18), lack of exclusive breastfeeding (OR: 2.34), more than 7 persons per household (OR: 1.96), exposure to indoor air pollution (OR: 1.57), incomplete immunization (OR: 1.83), undernutrition (OR: 4.47), and HIV infection (OR: 4.15). A

In developing countries, zinc supplementation in children younger than 5 years of age reduces the incidence of acute lower respiratory infection (IRR: 0.65) and was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of pneumonia. A
Pneumonia is a clinical diagnosis based on signs, symptoms, and clinical exam findings. C
Tachypnea is the best sign for identifying pneumonia in infants. C
The best individual measures in children younger than 5 years are oxygen saturation less than 94%, tachypnea, and retractions. C
Chest x-ray (CXR) is not recommended in children with mild uncomplicated acute lower respiratory tract infections.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Wheezing, upper respiratory symptoms, younger than 2 years, low-grade fever, hyperinflation; see chapter on bronchiolitis
History of recurrent wheezing or atopy, current wheezing; see chapter on asthma
History of choking or risk factors for aspiration (gastroesophageal reflux, neuromuscular disorders)
Age <3 years old, history of choking, unilateral or localized findings

list.listitem: See for typical presentations of community-acquired pneumonia.
The prevalence of radiographic pneumonia among children with clinically suspected pneumonia was 19% in North American studies and 37% in studies outside of North America.
Because of the overlap between presentations for different organisms, it is not possible to identify the causal pathogen on the basis of clinical presentation.

Any single clinical finding is not useful in determining if a child does or does not have pneumonia; combinations of clinical findings are more predictive. No single physical exam finding is useful in determining if a child under 5 years of age has pneumonia. Hypoxia (SpO2 <96%) and signs of increased work of breathing are most useful for diagnosis of pneumonia.

Distinguishing viral from bacterial pneumonia is difficult based on clinical symptoms alone. However, in children under five years of age hospitalized with community acquired pneumonia, the presence of wheezing has been noted to be an independent predictor of viral infection. A meta-analysis of 12 studies involving 7398 children with wheezing showed the following findings were associated with radiographic pneumonia: 1) temperature at least 38.4 degrees Celsius (LR+ 2.1, 95% CI 1.2-3.6), oxygen saturation less than 92% (LR+ 3.6, 95% CI 1.4-8.9), and grunting (LR+ 2.7, 95% CI 1.6-4.4).

Tachypnea is the best sign for identifying lower respiratory tract infections such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia in infants. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines tachypnea as a respiratory rate greater than 60 breaths per minute in children younger than 2 months, greater than 50 breaths per minute in children aged 2 to 12 months, and greater than 40 breaths per minute in children older than 12 months. The respiratory rate is more sensitive and specific in younger children. However, in older children a respiratory rate greater than 20 may still be consistent with pneumonia.

The best individual measures in children younger than 5 years are oxygen saturation less than 94%, tachypnea, and retractions. For children younger than 12 months, the best individual measure is nasal flaring.

In a prospective study of 570 children age 1 to 16 years with suspected pneumonia, the best independent predictors of an abnormal chest radiograph were fever (adjusted odds ratio 3.1), decreased breath sounds (aOR 1.5), the presence of crackles (aOR 2.0) and tachypnea (aOR 3.0).

In developed countries, a CXR is often obtained, but obtaining a CXR has not consistently been shown to alter management decisions, improve clinical outcomes, or differentiate viral from other etiologies. Therefore, several guidelines recommend no CXR in children with mild uncomplicated acute lower respiratory tract infections.
CXR findings can include consolidation or interstitial infiltrates; however, findings are not sensitive or specific for bacterial, atypical, or viral infections.

CXR may be useful if clinical findings are ambiguous, complications such as pleural effusion/empyema are suspected due to severity of disease or unresponsiveness to antimicrobial therapy, history of recurrent pneumonia or alternate diagnoses considered. There is lack of consensus regarding the need for lateral radiographs: The British Thoracic Society does not recommend routine lateral radiographs while the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends lateral CXRs in patients with hypoxemia, significant respiratory distress, antibiotic failure, or hospitalization for management of pneumonia.

There is an increase in the number of studies supporting the use of lung ultrasonography (LUS) to diagnose pneumonia and to evaluate complicated pneumonias. Recent studies demonstrate it to be as accurate as CXR or CT, and a recent meta-analysis demonstrated significantly better sensitivity with similar specificity of LUS when compared to CXR for the diagnosis of pediatric community-acquired pneumonia. Another recent meta-analysis demonstrated a pooled sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of pneumonia using LUS of 93% (95% CI, 88%-96%) and 96% (95% CI, 92%-98%), respectively. This modality has the advantage of reducing ionizing radiation and being more cost-effective than CT in evaluating complicated pneumonias, and is readily available. It has an excellent negative predictive value when normal and can thus exclude the need for antibiotics when negative.

Utility of LUS may be influenced by operator experience. In general, more experienced operators have higher diagnostic accuracy. Additional studies have shown excellent intraoperator reliability for detecting sonographic patterns on specific thoracic regions.

Optimal lung scanning by ultrasound should include posterior, anterior, and then lateral chest zones and be performed with both a transverse transducer orientation and a sagittal orientation. Omission of either orientation or any lung zone may decrease sensitivity of LUS. Specific lung ultrasound findings, such as the presence of deep and fixed air-liquid bronchograms, have been shown to correlate with development of complicated pneumonia and may be a useful tool to predict disease progression.

White blood cell (WBC) counts and inflammatory markers do not differentiate well between viral and bacterial pneumonia. Although, the average WBC count is higher in bacterial pneumonia than in viral, the degree of elevation does not reliably distinguish bacterial from viral infection. Consider a WBC count and differential only when adjunctive information is needed to help decide between bacterial and viral pneumonia.

Current guidelines recommend obtaining a blood culture in children hospitalized with moderate to severe pneumonia to potentially help guide antibiotic therapy, though this is based on low- to moderate-quality evidence. The prevalence of positive blood culture in children hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia in a 2015 systematic review was only 5.1%, with S. pneumoniae accounting for 77% of positives. In another large prospective study of children hospitalized with pneumonia, only 2.2% of children had bacteremia. The most common pathogens were S. pneumoniae (50%), S. aureus (13%), and S. pyogenes (4.9%). Predictors of bacteremia included male sex, presence of parapneumonic effusion, lack of wheezing, and no prior receipt of antibiotics. Children with bacteremia had significantly greater risk of ICU admission, increased need for mechanical ventilation, and overall longer duration of hospital stay.

Procalcitonin (PCT) has been proposed as a marker of bacterial pneumonia. Low values may be helpful in distinguishing viral pneumonia from bacterial. However, a systematic review found that the overall sensitivity and specificity of PCT in detecting bacterial pneumonia in children is low with sensitivity of 64% (95% CI, 53%-74%) and specificity of 72% (64%-79%). In patients with viral bronchiolitis, procalcitonin was unable to distinguish patients with bronchiolitis and concomitant bacterial coinfections, so procalcitonin must be taken in context of the full clinical picture. Further studies confirming the usefulness of PCT and a precise cut off level are needed. PCT may be helpful to obtain in cases of more severe disease (hospitalized) or to monitor treatment in complicated or severe pneumonia. PCT appears to be more accurate than C-reactive protein (CRP) and WBC counts in determining a viral versus bacterial etiology and evaluating severity. Serial measurement of procalcitonin in complicated or severe lower respiratory tract infections has been shown to assist with determining appropriate points for stopping antibiotic treatment without increasing adverse outcomes.

Serum copeptin levels were assessed in a study in Egypt, which found that serum copeptin levels were significantly elevated in pediatric patients with pneumonia when compared with healthy controls. Additionally, serum copeptin levels were found to be significantly higher in non-survivors compared to survivors of pediatric pneumonia.

A study found that presence of 3 clinical signs (focal decreased breath sounds, grunting, and absence of wheezing) with CRP >80mg/L and a positive serum pneumococcal PCR ruled in the diagnosis of complicated pneumonia (as defined by bacteremia, empyema, or pleural effusion) with a positive predictive value of 75%. In the absence of clinical signs with a low CRP, both complicated and uncomplicated pneumonia were unlikely (6% and 13%, respectively).
An economic analysis concluded that use of pulse oximetry in resource poor countries could significantly reduce the number of deaths due to pneumonia by identifying children with more severe disease.

Transcriptional profiling of leukocytes from peripheral blood specimens may assist with discrimination of community acquired pneumonia in children caused by viral, bacterial, or viral-bacterial coinfections. Further work is needed to bring this assay into practice to provide useful results within a clinically relevant timeframe.
See for additional studies indicated in selected patients.

A clinical prediction rule was developed and internally validated in 530 children who had a chest radiograph for suspected chest infection. Independent predictors of radiographic pneumonia included longer duration of fever, chills, nasal symptoms, abnormal chest exam, and O2 saturation <96%. The rule still requires prospective validation.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the child with suspected pneumonia.
Hospitalize children with respiratory distress, sustained hypoxia with SpO2 <90%, inability to tolerate oral intake, or other evidence of moderate to severe pneumonia.
Infants aged 1 to 3 months with afebrile pneumonia of infancy should be treated with a macrolide to cover C. pneumoniae. C

Children aged >4 months who are fully immunized and otherwise healthy should be treated with high-dose amoxicillin when a bacterial cause is suspected, and with a macrolide if an atypical pathogen is suspected. Antibiotic coverage should be broadened to a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime for the infant or child who is not fully immunized.B
Most children 3 months to 5 years old with pneumonia have viral etiologies which do not require antimicrobial therapy.B
See for recommendations regarding empiric antibiotic therapy in the outpatient and inpatient settings, by age and suspected pathogen.

Although it is difficult to differentiate between bacterial and viral pneumonia clinically and radiographically, apparent viral pneumonia should not be treated with antibiotics. For children with suspected atypical pneumonia (M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae), addition of azithromycin is recommended, with clarithromycin or erythromycin as alternatives. If atypical pneumonia is confirmed by laboratory testing, a macrolide alone is recommended.
A Danish study found poor compliance with guidelines recommending narrow spectrum antibiotics for firstline therapy of childhood pneumonia in the hospital.
Most preschool-aged children with pneumonia have a viral etiology; antimicrobials are not recommended for viral pneumonia.
There is no clear evidence to support the effectiveness of antitussives in children.

A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine the efficacy of a macrolide antibiotic versus a non-macrolide antibiotic in the treatment of M. pneumoniae associated pneumonia. However, one study of children with recurrent respiratory infections found that when the lower respiratory tract infection was associated with Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, or both by PCR and/or paired sera, children treated with azithromycin were more likely to have clinical resolution of symptoms after 1 month compared to those treated with no azithromycin. Routine empirical use of a macrolide in addition to β- lactam therapy for children hospitalized with community acquired-pneumonia has not shown a benefit in children.

Italian multisociety guidelines (2024) recommend a 5 day course of amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day divided in 3 doses as first-line for fully vaccinated children. A macrolide should be added in children over 5 years if response to amoxicillin is poor or they are penicillin allergic.

In children with Mycoplasma infection, early treatment within the first 36 hours of hospitalization with corticosteroids was associated with significant clinical improvement and reduced disease progression, with no added benefit from macrolide therapy.

In a randomized trial, ceftaroline was similarly effective to ceftriaxone in hospitalized infants and children with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. Adverse events were similar, although Coombs seroconversion was common with ceftaroline (17%).
While prompt initiation of antibiotics is generally recommended, a large retrospective cohort study found no difference in outcomes for children treated within 1 day and those who were not.

A study in Pakistan identified 4002 children age 2 months to 59 months with cough and tachypnea. Those with red flags for severe pneumonia or with O2 saturation <90% were excluded. They were randomized to 3 days of weight-dosed amoxicillin twice daily or placebo. There was no clinically meaningful difference in treatment failure rates between groups (4.8% for placebo, 2.5% with amoxicillin, p <0.05). Children with higher respiratory rates and fever were more likely to experience treatment failure.
There is uncertain evidence regarding vitamin A for prevention of acute lower respiratory tract infections in children, and no evidence to support it for treatment.
There is no evidence to support vitamin D for prevention of pneumonia.

In a study from Uganda, zinc adjunct therapy (in addition to antibiotics), reduced mortality in children with severe pneumonia compared to placebo (RR: 0.33; 95% CI, 0.15-0.76). This is more effective in children with HIV.

A prospective, randomized controlled trial of children less than 5 years of age hospitalized with pneumonia in Pakistan examined the impact of zinc supplementation on clinical symptoms. There were no statistically signficant improvements in clinical symptoms in children receiving zinc supplementation. However, hospital length of stay was significantly shorter among children receiving zinc compared with children not supplemented with zinc.
Hypoxic patients should be treated with oxygen. Nasal prongs and nasopharyngeal catheters are equally effective.
Children who are unable to maintain their fluid intake or are dehydrated should be treated with intravenous fluids.

Patients receiving intravenous fluids should have their electrolyte levels monitored for inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone, resulting in hyponatremia. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is treated with fluid restriction, treatment of the underlying cause (pneumonia), and can include administration of sodium chloride.

Antipyretics and analgesics may be considered to keep the patient comfortable, if necessary, but excessive use should be discouraged. There is emerging evidence that pre-hospital NSAID treatment may be associated with a greater risk of complicated pneumonia in adults and children. Possible reasons include NSAID-mediated inhibition of inflammatory responses and neutrophil recruitment, delay in seeking medical care, and delay in initiation of antibiotic treatment.
Chest physiotherapy is not effective in children with pneumonia.
For afebrile pneumonia of infancy, the duration of therapy is 14 days for erythromycin or 5 days for azithromycin to cover C. pneumoniae.
In older infants and children, uncomplicated infection has traditionally been treated for 7 days; the course for azithromycin is 5 days.

Two recent meta-analyses have demonstrated the non-inferiority of short-course (3- or 5-day) oral antibiotic treatment for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in children. The first evaluated treatment failure in 10,662 participants (98% of whom were 2 to 59 months of age) with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia across eight randomized clinical trials, finding a 3-day course of oral antibiotic therapy was noninferior to a 5-day course (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.91-1.12), and a 5-day course was non-inferior to a 10-day course (RR 0.87; 95% CI 0.50-1.53). The second focused on treatment of 12,774 outpatients in 16 different randomized clinical trials, showing a lack of substantial difference between shorter duration (5 days or less) and longer duration antibiotic treatment in overall clinical cure (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.17), treatment failure (RR 1.06,95% CI 0.93-1.21), or relapse (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.92-1.35).
See for indications for hospital admission.
For drug allergies, comorbid conditions, treatment failure, recurrent infections, or complications, consider referral to infectious disease or pulmonology specialists.
The management of effusions or empyema may require surgical consultation.

Failure to improve in 48 to 72 hours may be due to misdiagnosis, ineffective antibiotic coverage, or development of complications. Misdiagnosis: review history and physical and consider repeat CXR and laboratory testing. Ineffective antibiotic coverage: consider changing or adding antibiotics or using intravenous antibiotics. Development of complications: obtain repeat CXR to look for pleural effusion or empyema. Mild pleural effusions can be monitored with CXR, but enlarging or compromising effusions may require further imaging, drainage, fibrinolytic therapy, or surgery.
Closely monitor the vital signs, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, auscultatory findings, and hydration status of hospitalized patients.
In children hospitalized for pneumonia, 1% to 5% of children develop effusion; less than 1% develop empyema; and 1% develop concurrent bacteremia. A
The in-hospital case fatality rate is 0.2% to 0.4%. A
The incidence of hospitalization for pneumonia per 1000 persons per year is 7.9 for children younger than 2 years, 3.4 for children aged 2 to 4 years, and 0.7 for children aged 5 to 17 years.
In children hospitalized for pneumonia, 1% to 5% of children develop effusion; less than 1% develop empyema; and 1% develop concurrent bacteremia.
The in-hospital case fatality ratio is 0.2% to 0.4%.

In one study, 5.5% of children with pneumonia have major sequelae including restrictive lung disease, obstructive lung disease or bronchiectasis with restrictive lung disease being the most common sequelae at 13.6% (95% CI, 6.2%-21.1%).

Risk factors independently associated with mortality and poor clinical outcomes for children admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) were the presence of comorbidities, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and bacteremia.
For acute uncomplicated pneumonia, a follow up CXR is not necessary.
Consider follow up CXR for children with recurrent pneumonias in the same lobe, lobar collapse, apparent round pneumonia, pleural effusion, pneumatoceles, or pulmonary abscess after 4 to 6 weeks.
Families should be educated about fever/pain management, maintaining hydration, and signs of deterioration.

cell.label: START Initial clinical findings suggestive of CAP in age >1 month
Assess clinical signs and symptoms: - Respiratory rate for age above threshold - Fever >38ºC - O2 saturation less than 94% - Nasal flaring - Abnormal breath sounds - Increased work of breathing.
Measure respiratory rate (RR) by observation for 60 seconds when the child is awake and not crying. Tachypnea is: 1 to 12 months old: RR >50 1 to 5 years old: RR > 40 > 5 years old: RR >20.
Pneumonia not suspected, manage as appropriate.
Suspect viral infection. Consider diagnosis and treatment of influenza. Supportive treatment, no antibiotics needed. Monitor closely for possible bacterial/missed pneumonia.
Ambiguous clinical findings or age younger than 5 years with high fever of uncertain source.
Complication suspected or prolonged course unresponsive to antibiotics.
Consider: CXR, procalcitonin and WBC with differential.
Suspect viral pneumonia. Consider treatment of influenza in appropriate seasons. Supportive treatment, no antibiotics needed. Monitor closely for possible bacterial/ missed pneumonia.
Manage for specific complication. Consider infectious disease and/or pulmonology consult.
Follow up as appropriate. Adjust antibiotic, if necessary.

feature.caption: Typical Presentation of CAP.
feature.feature_body:
Bacterial pneumonia Fever >38ºC, cough, tachypnea, retractions, hypoxia, may appear toxic, localized crackles, diminished breath sounds
Atypical pneumonia School age, headache, malaise, gradually worsening nonproductive cough, low-grade fever, may have wheezing
Viral pneumonia Age <5 years, fever >38.5ºC, viral prodrome, respiratory rate normal or raised, may have wheezing
Because of the overlap between presentations for different organisms, it is not possible to identify the causal pathogen on the basis of clinical presentation or radiographs.

tr.td: CXR
Not needed for uncomplicated pneumonia, see
Not consistently shown to alter management decisions, improve clinical outcomes, or differentiate viral from other etiologies.
Lung ultrasonography
Not needed for uncomplicated pneumonia, see Figure 1
May aid in the diagnosis of pneumonia and the evaluation of complicated pneumonias. No ionizing radiation. More cost effective than CT.
WBC
Not needed for uncomplicated pneumonia, see

White blood cell counts and inflammatory markers do not differentiate between viral and bacterial pneumonia. Although the average WBC is higher in bacterial pneumonia than in viral (18,000 vs 13,000), the degree of elevation does not reliably distinguish bacterial from viral infection.
Acute phase reactants (PCT and CRP)
Not needed for uncomplicated pneumonia, see

Studies suggesting the usefulness of PCT in the diagnosis and management of pediatric CAP are multiple but further studies are needed and a precise cut off level has not been defined. Low values may be helpful in distinguishing viral pneumonia from bacterial pneumonia. May obtain if more severe disease (hospitalized). May be helpful to monitor treatment in complicated or severe pneumonia. PCT appears to be more effective than CRP for determining a viral versus bacterial etiology and evaluating severity.
Blood culture
Consider in severe, resistant, or unusual forms of pneumonia
More helpful before antibiotics started. Unlikely to be positive in patients well enough to be treated as outpatients.
Rapid viral studies
May decrease the need for additional diagnostic studies and antibiotic use
Patients can have mixed infections or bacterial superinfections of an initially viral process.
Sputum gram stain and culture
Obtain if more severe disease (hospitalized)
Difficult to obtain in young children.
Pleural cultures
Useful if patient has pleural effusion
More helpful before antibiotics started.
PPD
Obtain if patient is at high risk of exposure
Mycoplasma PCR C. pneumoniae Urinary antigen testing Culture of throat swab
Recommended if suspected Not recommended Not recommended Not recommended
Can help guide choice of antibiotics. Reliable testing is not available. False positive tests are common. Likely to reflect oral flora.

feature.caption: Empiric Antibiotic Treatment for Bacterial Pneumonia.

tr.td: <3 months
IV ceftriaxone or IV cefotaxime
3 months to 5 years

First-line: High-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day divided bid) Alternative: amoxicillin-clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day bid Penicillin allergy: Clindamycin Presumed atypical infection (M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae): azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day day 1 and 5 mg/kg/day days 2-5. Clarithromycin or erythromycin are alternatives. Presumed influenza pneumonia: oseltamivir If treatment failure with amoxicillin: consider resistance, atypical infection such as M. pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae, viral infection or complications of LRTI such as empyema

All ages, fully immunized, presumed bacterial pneumonia, and minimal local resistance to invasive pneumococcus strains: First line: Ampicillin or penicillin G Alternatives: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, add vancomycin or clindamycin if community-acquired MRSA is suspected. Atypical pneumonia: azithromycin If atypical pneumonia cannot be excluded: add azithromycin to a beta-lactam. Alternatives include clarithromycin, erythromycin, and if > 7 years old doxycycline. Levofloxacin if growth maturity and cannot tolerate a macrolide. Presumed influenza pneumonia: oseltamivir or zanamivir. All ages, not fully immunized for H flu, s pneumonia, or significant local resistance to invasive pneumococcal strains: First line: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (alternative: levofloxacin); add vancomycin or clindamycin if CA-MRSA suspected Atypical pneumonia: azithromycin If atypical pneumonia cannot be excluded: add azithromycin to a beta-lactam. Alternatives include clarithromycin, erythromycin, and if > 7 years old doxycycline. Levofloxacin if growth maturity and cannot tolerate a macrolide. Presumed influenza pneumonia: oseltamivir or zanamivir.
Older than 5 years

First-line: High-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day divided bid) Penicillin allergy: Clindamycin If unclear from lab or imaging whether bacterial or atypical bacterial pathogen: amoxicillin/clavulanate AND azithromycin Presumed atypical infection (M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae): azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day to max of 500 mg on day 1, 5 mg/kg/day to max 250 mg on days 2-5. Clarithromycin or erythromycin are alternatives (or doxycycline if >7 years old).
